title: Quoting Scott Aaronson
text: It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved. — Scott Aaronson Tags: mathematics , llms , ai , generative-ai

title: The Revolution vs The Renaissance — Thariq Shihipar, OpenAI
author: Latent.Space
text: AI can make software cheap enough to produce by the thousand and still give you more time to make one thing feel right. At AI Engineer CODE, Thariq Shihipar shows how those two futures can coexist. In his fighting game, he edits the size of a rock in the /human folder and immediately tries the throw. He also built a Mac Dock that switched modes, used it, and realized he cared more about noticing when he got distracted. We get into what Thariq changed his mind about with coding agents, how a decision model can choose from actions a designer defines, and who gets to decide which experiments deserve the compute. Thariq announced his move to OpenAI after we recorded. Sponsored by Jira by Atlassian. Learn more at jira.dev . title: [AINews] Math Proofs Are Landing Faster Than We Can Read Them
author: swyx .ai
text: AINews by Latent Space Scott Aaronson was still trying to digest two proofs of VP ≠ VNP at dinner. Before dessert, an OpenAI paper claimed that the square matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4 . During dessert, another paper claimed matching upper and lower bounds for the finite Fourier transform . The lower bound is the biggest news. In October, OpenAI found an upper bound for ω down to at most 9/4 . Finding the lower bound = upper bound leaves only one possible value, which is a shocking result for most. We plotted 64 selected AI-assisted research advances so far this year. November accounts for 20, including six preprints from Google’s Cogentic . The curve follows public releases, including proofs still under review. We count the two VP ≠ VNP proofs once and give October’s faster matrix multiplication algorithm and November’s matching lower bound an entry each. The big releases underline how much a paper count can hide. OpenAI’s catalogue lists 730 manuscripts across 375 result families, including follow-ups and companion arguments. Its revision log also records three October withdrawals after a sign error in one paper affected two others. Yupan Liu showed that two messages suffice for quantum interactive proofs , a result that would have been a big deal on its own. Aaronson says Liu used AI and that he had to remind himself the result had even happened. In other big news, today’s guest Thariq Shihipar announced his big move from Anthropic to OpenAI , the second high profile Ant→OAI move in recent times after Cat Wu . We dive into his two philosophies of AI and how and where /humans add taste. AI News for 11/25/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap AI-Generated Math Results: Matmul Exponent, Factoring and Lean Proofs Matrix multiplication exponent : OpenAI's model claims a lower bound matching its October upper bound, making ω exactly 9/4. Previously no nontrivial lower bound was known ( @SebastienBubeck ; repo ). Mechanism : The result reportedly comes through an explicit superlinear circuit lower bound ( @wjmzbmr1 ). Implications : Bubeck notes that a prior Lee et al. result implies LPs solvable in n^{9/4}. He also says LPs can now be solved in strongly polynomial time, a Smale problem ( follow-up ). Expert reaction : Omri Weinstein calls it "truly surreal" if correct, since most experts expected ω = 2 ( @WeinsteinOmri ). OpenAI batch : Nine new papers with Lean proofs came out a day after a claimed VP ≠ VNP proof ( summary ). Other claims : Fourier transform complexity of n√log n ( @lreyzin ). Integer multiplication : Also n√log n, tight under weak ETH ( @cloneofsimo ). Same-day solutions : Anthropic posted its own VP ≠ VNP solution the same day ( @vitaliychiley ). Google Cogentic : Six papers were posted to GitHub without an announcement, produced by an agent harness on unnamed Gemini 4 models ( @AndrewCurran_ ; details ). Results : A proven NFS-class factoring bound, beating a 1992 record. Also claimed: Deterministic subexponential factoring. Faster small-characteristic discrete log. A 1/5 Nash approximation. Progress below the square-root barrier on log-rank. Edge reconstruction for linear-density graphs. Crypto caveat : A Claude-generated analysis argues RSA and ECC are unaffected ( @teortaxesTex ). title: Why Linear says Issue Tracking is Dead — Cristina Cordova, COO
author: Latent.Space
text: Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. title: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
author: 0x23
text: Hi all, I am a professor in algorithm engineering. In our field we use a method of falsifiable hypothesis testing to improve algorithms. More precisely, this is a cycle consisting of designing an algorithm, analyzing the algorithm, then implementing it and lastly testing it using experiments on real-world instances which leads to designing new algorithms based on the current observations. We put this methodology into an AI skill which runs in an infinite loop. This skill first creates a performance profile, then produces a hypothesis which is implemented and tested automatically using an AI agent. If the change improved the performance and tests negotiated with the user verify it, the change is kept, if not it is discarded. Everything is tracked via version control. Part of the output is a pdf report which documents all the code changes and progress over time as well as individual patches to only merge specific patches if one chooses to do so. Moreover, this comes with a knowledge-base in which we collect global optimization knowledge, thereby improving the skill over time. We ran this on a wide range of public code bases, e.g. our KaHIP graph partitioning toolkit, which improved running time by 3.9x, or our VieCut minimum cut solver, where the skill improved the running time of the system by 8.9x; I do believe the skill is very easy to use and hence am sharing this here. Let me know what you think!

title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
author: bjin
text: Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were. 11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence", https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/ ) described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week? So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution: g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n] There is a dedicated section for this: https://bjin.github.io/go-codegolf-benchmark/#why/finding-a-... It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models. Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem from a different angle. It also rewards running experiments, not just thinking: writing a search program to find a shorter expression, or exploring lesser-known features and functions in the target compiler, interpreter, or library. Human code golfers do this a lot, and no public training data tells a frontier model how to do so.
